title: Facts Before Fury
author: Weber County Sheriff Ryan Arbon
paragraphs: Truth before pride. Principle before politics.
Freedom, justice, and the rule of law depend on something we cannot afford to lose: our commitment to truth.
I believe one of the greatest responsibilities we share as Americans is the willingness to seek the truth, even when it challenges what we think we know or want to do.
Today, we are surrounded by headlines, short videos, social media posts, and strong opinions. Information travels in seconds, and it is easy to form a conclusion before we understand the whole story.
But what if we paused? What if, instead of rushing to judgment, we took the time to ask questions, examine the evidence, and listen to perspectives different from our own?
Being convinced we are right does not necessarily mean we have the facts right. The pursuit of truth requires both courage and humility.

Truth is not owned by a political party, an ideology, or an individual. It is something we must work to discover. That means being willing to look beyond convenient explanations, consider information that challenges our assumptions, and change our minds when the evidence leads us somewhere unexpected.
This matters especially when the issues involve public safety, constitutional rights, elections, or the actions of our fellow citizens.
Incomplete information can lead to misunderstandings.

Misunderstandings can create distrust. And when distrust is fueled by frustration, anger, and misinformation, it can divide relationships and communities and, in some circumstances, contribute to hatred and violence.
Our words matter. What we share matters. And the care we take to establish the facts matters.

We have every right to question government, challenge public officials, express our beliefs, assemble peacefully, and demand accountability. Those freedoms are fundamental to our Constitution and worth defending.

We also have an opportunity to exercise those freedoms wisely. Before sharing an accusation or condemning someone, we can verify the information, seek original sources, and ask whether we truly understand the circumstances.
When wrongdoing occurs, we should pursue accountability through fair and lawful means. When the facts prove our assumptions wrong, we should have the integrity to acknowledge it.
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. said, “The time is always right to do what is right.”
Doing what is right sometimes means standing firm. Other times, it means listening, reconsidering, or admitting we were mistaken. Both require character.

I swore an oath to support and defend our Constitution because I believe in what it makes possible: a nation where liberty is protected, government is accountable, and people with different beliefs can live together under the rule of law.

I believe most Americans want safe communities, honest government, fair treatment, and the freedom to live according to their convictions. We may disagree about how to achieve those things, but we do not have to become enemies in the process.
We can disagree without hatred, demand accountability without abandoning fairness, and defend our principles without diminishing the dignity of others.
Imagine what we could accomplish if we cared more about finding the truth than proving ourselves right.
Facts before fury. Truth before pride. Principle before politics.
We cannot control everything others say or do. But we can choose to be thoughtful in what we believe, responsible in what we share, and respectful in how we treat others.
A free society depends on citizens who have the courage to seek the truth, the humility to learn, and the resolve to do what is right once the truth is known.
Let us be the kind of citizens who strengthen our communities, preserve our freedoms, and leave the next generation a country better than the one we inherited.
That begins with each of us.

title: Delegitimizing Ogden Valley's Namesake
author: Dave Martin
paragraphs: A response to the Guest Commentary published in the October 15, Ogden Valley News entitled – In His Own Hand: The History Behind Our City's Name, by Gordon Auchincloss (GA)

If there's one thing we know about history, it's that history is complicated and repeats itself. Many historians argue that judging the past by today's standards distorts our understanding of why events happened. Evaluating historical figures like Peter Skene Ogden without understanding the context of his specific social, economic, and cultural realities ignores the forces that shaped his decisions. It assumes that modern society has achieved ultimate moral clarity, ignoring the fact that future generations will likely judge our current actions just as harshly. Reducing complex historical figures like Mr. Ogden to simple "good" or "bad" labels prevents us from learning how deeply flawed individuals were still able to achieve historic advancements and make significant contributions.

In a well-crafted article, GA clearly paints Peter Skene Ogden as a “bad” man as perceived through the lens of contemporary moral sensibilities. Was Ogden really involved in the murder of an indigenous man? Did he verbalize and publish threats of extermination against the Snake Indians (men)? Did he deliberately trap beaver to near extinction? During the fur trade era, were there lots of other historical individuals, dynamics and influences driving these narratives? Yes, to each question.

The competition during the fur trade was relentless and violent, often kill or be killed. The Snake, Blackfeet and other tribes routinely attacked and killed trappers, stealing their horses, guns, traps and gear. There was seldom any love lost between western tribes and fur trapping mountain men. Retaliation was often used as payback and deterrence. Can you imagine conducting the business of trapping beaver in the otherwise unforgiving environment of the western frontier, facing unimaginable deprivations of cold and starvation under the constant threat of death? Do you think you might have expressed some negative sentiment towards your assailants? These days social media and pop music lyrics are rife with published threats of violence and hatred for just having a different opinion. Assassinations and murders are encouraged and cheered on when they occur. Many are indifferent, just ignore or laugh it off. And, we think we have some kind of moral high ground to pass judgment on history?

The harm to indigenous peoples, particularly the Shoshone, alleged by over-trapping beaver is greatly overstated in GA's article. The Snake tribes, when not attacking trappers, were otherwise substantially involved, if not complicit, in the fur trade and benefited by trading beaver for European and North American trade goods – iron cookware, traps, guns, horses...

As for the two schools GA cites as removing Ogden's name, the action seems more the result of virtue signaling than thorough and fair “homework.” Some examples of Ogden's more unexamined, or otherwise ignored, nobler character follow here-

On May 8, 1825, in present day Cache Valley, just before arriving at future Ogden Valley, Mr. Ogden graciously allowed four lodges of Snake Indians to join with his brigade for their own protection against the Blackfeet.

In 1818 Peter Skene Ogden married a Flathead Indian woman raising 7 children (an 8th child died in infancy) staying true to her for the duration of his life, notwithstanding, most country marriages when many trappers, upon retirement, abandoned their Indian wife and children when leaving the territory.

In 1847, During the Whitman Massacre, where 13 individuals were murdered, Peter Skene Ogden was the key figure to arrange and facilitate the release and saving the lives of 45 hostages through a trade goods ransom. The hostages were then evacuated to Fort Vancouver and returned to Oregon City in early January 1848.

According to GA, “Two elected bodies [school boards] read the [Peter Skene Ogden] record and acted [removed Ogden's name]. Ours [Ogden City Council] did not.” Apparently, our city council didn't know there was an obligation to have Peter Skene Ogden biographical expertise to legitimize their decision to continue the use of an established valley namesake. Rather wisely, the council actually made their decision resting more on the potential hardship and economic impact business owners and residents would bare themselves, among other unintended consequences, in using a new name.

GA concludes his article by browbeating and guilting the Ogden Valley City Council for being such historical slackers and subverting the will of Valley residents by not adopting a new municipal name based on the outcome of the Name Our New City survey. To be clear and honest, in spite of the fervor in conducting the survey, many valley residents suspect clarity and honesty were missing. It is important to realize polls and surveys assess preferences and establish rankings. They are notoriously biased and skewed in their sampling. They do not have the legal standing of a ballot initiative, no matter how fervent the desired outcome of those conducting the polls and surveys. And, if not voted on, the final decision rests with our city council as it should. Fare and square.

While giving the city a new name is said to only cost the city $500, it will cost businesses currently using the Ogden Valley name as part of their own business name considerably more with the added confusion of a new name basically superimposed over the same geographic area represented by the name Ogden Valley. Neither is it reasonable to expect that such Ogden Valley businesses take on the hardship and expense of rebranding to accommodate a new city name.
Agreeing with GA, it would be worthwhile for Ogden Valley residents desiring a better understanding of Mr. Ogden's contribution to our Ogden Valley heritage to read his journal.

A link to those journals can be found at – OgdenHole.com And, with all due respect, GA might revisit Ogden's journals himself, along with his clerk William Kittson's journal with a little more fair and balanced attention, and less cherry picking to drive a new name narrative. We have an awesome Ogden Valley pre-settlement heritage above and beyond however people are determined to judge Mr. Ogden's values or morals. It includes the very first primary source descriptions of Shoshone interaction. And, believe it or not, it was amicable!

For 10 years running Ogden Valley 200 (OV200) successfully sponsored well attended annual history seminars for Ogden Valley residents every May, inviting the participation of local historians, leaders of the NWB of the Shoshone Nation, and direct descendants of Peter Skene Ogden himself. Each of these presenters provided unique and relevant perspectives of our Ogden Valley heritage. There might well be some Ogden Valley residents that have more local historical background than GA gives them credit for even though our city council, as suggested in GA's article, is notably clueless. We forgive our city council for this gross oversight and greatly appreciate their attention to far more pressing issues in bringing our new city up to speed.
All this being said, and so there's no misunderstanding, I actually quite like and respect GA (aka: my friend Gordon). We spin together at HEL Fitness. I just question his spin on this one.

title: In His Own Hand: The History Behind Our City's Name
author: Gordon Auchincloss
paragraphs: “Acting for myself, I will not hesitate to say I would willingly sacrifice a year or two to exterminate the whole Snake tribe, women and children excepted. In so doing I could fully justify myself before God and man.”

Those words were written in 1828, in an official Hudson’s Bay Company expedition journal. The journal survives in the Company’s archives and was published by the Oregon Historical Society more than a century ago. The man who wrote it was offering two years of his life to destroy a people.
His name was Peter Skene Ogden. Our city is named after him.

When our council voted on July 30 to keep the name Ogden Valley City, “honoring our history” was offered from the dais as a leading reason. I have already written in these pages about my concerns regarding the process behind that vote. This letter is about the history itself, because it appears that no one on the council ever read it.

Here is what the record shows: In 1816 Ogden was a clerk for the Northwest Company. He led a party of his men to a rival Hudson’s Bay Company post and forced the clerk there to surrender an Indigenous man named Le Boeuf (Buffalo), whose apparent offense was trading with that company. They killed him within sight of the post’s walls. A Hudson’s Bay officer recorded in his post journal that Ogden and his men “butchered him in a most cruel manner,” and he described Ogden’s personal hand in the killing. That was the judgment of Ogden’s own contemporaries, in the most brutal industry on the continent. Four men gave sworn depositions concerning the murder, and on that record a court at Montreal found a bill of indictment for murder against Ogden. The proceedings are preserved in papers printed for the British House of Commons.

Ogden never answered the charge. He ran from it, and his employer arranged the running: while the Hudson’s Bay Company pursued the indictment, the Northwest Company, whose trade war the killing served, promoted Ogden and transferred him across the Rockies, beyond the practical reach of the courts. When the two warring companies merged in 1821, the company that had sought his indictment hired him anyway, and his career flourished.

The extermination proposal quoted above was not a stray outburst. A year earlier, on a different expedition, Ogden wrote the same doctrine into his 1826-27 journal: “We all know Indians are treacherous, bloodthirsty. The sooner the exterminating system be introduced among them, the better.” Twice, two years apart, in business records kept for his employers to read, he proposed annihilation of Indian tribes as policy. Men say ugly things in anger. They do not write them into the company’s books twice, with a timeline and an offer to carry the work out personally.

These were also the years of the Hudson’s Bay Company’s “fur desert” policy, which Ogden carried out across the Snake Country. The mandate was in writing before his first brigade ever left. Governor George Simpson wrote in his 1824 journal that the Snake Country was “a rich preserve of Beaver” and one “which for political reasons we should endeavor to destroy as fast as possible,” so that American trappers, the advance guard of American settlement, would find nothing worth coming for.

This was not trapping for a livelihood. It was deliberate annihilation of beavers as strategy, and it required the Company to abandon its own practices. In its own territories the Company enforced conservation: quotas, closed seasons, rules against taking cubs and summer pelts, because a trapped-out country was bad business. In the Snake Country those rules were suspended on purpose. Extirpation spares nothing, not the breeding females and not the kits in the lodge. The Company knew how to keep beaver on the land. Here the object was to kill every last one.

The first expedition sent out under that mandate entered this valley in May 1825, the same visit that mapped it and left Ogden’s name on it. The man our city honors first came here to empty this place of a natural resource. That should mean something in a valley that now understands what beavers are: the engineers of wetlands, the keepers of water on dry land, a species our own state wildlife agency relocates into damaged watersheds to repair them. And the beaver were not the only ones who depended on living streams. Emptied land starves the people who live on it, and the people who lived on it were indigenous people. Destroying the beaver and destroying the people were not unrelated ideas. The first was Company policy, which Ogden willingly followed. The second was Ogden's offer to go further on his own.

And here is the part that should stop every resident of our valley: the “Snakes” of Ogden’s journals are the Shoshone — the indigenous people of this place. The Northwestern Shoshone lived in this valley for centuries before any trapper arrived; at the July 30 meeting, their name for it — “where the red berries grow” — was warmly invoked from the dais as part of the heritage the current name supposedly honors. No one in that room appeared to know that the namesake proposed, in his own hand, to exterminate the Shoshone people — that the man honored in the name and the people honored in the speech stand on opposite sides of the same sentence in his journal.

None of this is hidden. Finding it took me one evening with published primary sources. Others have done the same homework and acted on it. In 2021, the school board in Oregon City, the town where Ogden died, voted unanimously to take his name off a middle school. Last year, a district in Vancouver, Washington, removed his Christian name from an elementary school, finding that the man’s history did not match the school’s values. Two elected bodies read the record and acted. Ours did not know the record existed.

I want to be clear about what I am not arguing. The valley will be called Ogden Valley whatever the city is named. No one proposes otherwise, and two centuries of maps are safe. Nor am I asking the council to adopt my judgment of the man. They are free to form their own opinion. My question is narrower. How does a council pass a resolution permanently “settling” a name for generations, in the name of history, without one sentence of inquiry into the history in question? A murder indictment and a written proposal of extermination of indigenous people are not footnotes. They are the kind of facts due diligence begs to find.

Our city is not a year old. It had, and still has, something Oregon City’s school board did not: a blank slate, a change the city itself estimated costing $500, and a community on record wanting to choose a different name. The question was never whether to erase history. It is whether a brand-new city’s first permanent act of commemoration should honor a man whose history and handwriting argue against it.
Read the history. Read Ogden’s own journals. Then tell me the name is settled.

title: Patriot Day, September 11, 2026
author: Don Hickman
paragraphs: Lest we forget—2,977 innocent lives were taken on September 11, 2001. America went to war that day, against an amorphous enemy who hated us for who we are and what we represent.

Twenty-five years ago, I was an Air Force Major on the Pentagon’s Air Staff, serving as the counter-chemical, biological, and radiological terrorism war planner. My team and I were in a classified facility in Washington, D.C., watching the news as the World Trade Center North Tower burned. Then, live on TV, United Flight 175 struck the South Tower.

Thirty-four minutes later, American Flight 77 struck the Pentagon, and we heard the explosion even in our secure facility. We stepped outside and saw smoke rising above that gigantic building. Soon came the word that United Flight 93 had crashed in Pennsylvania.
It was clear to us - this was our Pearl Harbor moment. America had been attacked, and we were at war.

After the initial shock, I called Stacey, as she was getting our one-year-old ready for a post-surgery follow-up at Walter Reed Army Medical Center.  I remember confusion when she asked why I said don’t leave the house, and these words I said to her:

“Turn on the TV.  We’ve been attacked and are going to war.  I’m OK.  I love you the two of you.  Call the family and tell them I’m alive and OK.  I don’t know when I’ll be home.  Don’t leave the house until I let you know it’s safe.”
It would be four days before I got home.
The planning staff returned to the Pentagon a few days after the attack.  The smell of aviation fuel and acrid smoke permeated the building. I’ll never forget the smell and what it represented.

Over the months that followed Stacey bore the heavy burden at home while I worked 18+-hour days on the Air Force Crisis Action Team, protecting the homeland and ensuring our warfighters had what they needed to carry the fight to al-Qaeda - across Afghanistan, the Arabian Peninsula, Asia, and Africa.

September 11, now known as Patriot Day, is very personal for me. In addition to my first-hand experience in the Pentagon, my friend and U.S. Air Force Academy classmate, Leroy Homer, was the First Officer of United Flight 93. He was murdered in the cockpit as terrorists seized the plane.

The other 2,976 victims came from across the United States and 90 other countries - from every walk of life, every political party, every race, every religion, and every creed. I lament that it took the tragedy of 9/11 to unite us - and that today, as a nation, and to a certain extent our Valley, we are again so divided.

Today we remember. We reflect. Together, let's unite and create our future Ogden Valley.
​
Note: Don Hickman retired as a Colonel from the Air Force in 2012 with over 25 years of active-duty service.  As a City Council member, he represents District 5 and serves as Mayor Pro Tempore.  Over the past eight months, he has administered Public Works and Engineering while also co-chairing the Agriculture Committee.
